items.stem: Mohammed writes: "The more people who witness an emergency, the more likely the victim is to be helped." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Each individual is less likely to help as group size increases (bystander effect); in some real emergencies, though, the larger number of bystanders makes it more likely at least one person helps (Philpot et al., 2020).

items.stem: With reference to Piliavin, Rodin and Piliavin (1969), explain how research has investigated the arousal-cost-reward model of helping.
items.answer: Piliavin, Rodin and Piliavin (1969). Aim: to investigate the effect of victim characteristics on helping in a natural setting. Method: A confederate collapsed in a New York subway carriage, appearing either ill (carrying a cane) or drunk (smelling of alcohol); observers recorded helping in about 4,450 passengers. Findings: the ill victim was helped spontaneously on 95% of trials and the drunk victim on about 50%; there was no diffusion of responsibility Link: the arousal-cost-reward model of helping.

items.stem: Explain the arousal-cost-reward model.
items.answer: Seeing an emergency causes unpleasant arousal; bystanders weigh the costs of helping (danger, effort, disgust) and of not helping (guilt, blame) and choose the response that reduces arousal most cheaply, so a "drunk" victim is helped less (higher cost, less blame for not helping).

items.stem: With reference to Toi and Batson (1982), explain how research has investigated empathy-based altruism.

items.stem: Describe the study by Darley and Latané (1968) and explain what it shows about diffusion of responsibility in bystanderism.
items.answer: Darley and Latané (1968). Aim: to investigate whether the number of bystanders affects helping in an emergency. Method: 72 New York University students took part in a discussion over an intercom, believing there were 1, 2 or 5 people in the group; one "participant" (a recording) appeared to have a seizure. Findings: 85% of those who thought they were alone helped before the end of the seizure, compared with 31% of those who thought four others were present Link: diffusion of responsibility in bystanderism.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for accurate description of the study (aim, method, findings: 85% of those who thought they were alone helped before the end of the seizure, compared with 31% of those who thought four others were present); up to 2 marks for explicitly linking the findings to diffusion of responsibility in bystanderism. A study that is described but not linked cannot score more than half marks.

items.stem: Which research method best describes the study by Toi and Batson (1982) on empathy and helping "Carol"?
options: meta-analysis
covert participant observation
laboratory experiment
natural experiment
items.answer: laboratory experiment
items.markingKey: C. Toi and Batson (1982): Students listened to a radio interview with "Carol", a student who had broken both legs and was behind in a course; empathy was manipulated by instructions, and the cost of not helping was varied by whether Carol would be in their class.

items.stem: Using Sprafkin, Liebert and Poulos (1975) as supporting evidence, explain promoting prosocial behaviour through modelling.
items.answer: Sprafkin, Liebert and Poulos (1975). Aim: to investigate whether watching prosocial television increases helping in children. Method: First-grade children watched one of three TV episodes: a "Lassie" episode in which a boy rescues a puppy, a neutral "Lassie" episode, or a family sitcom; they were then given a choice between helping distressed puppies or playing a game for points. Findings: children who watched the prosocial episode spent much longer helping the puppies than children in the other conditions Link: promoting prosocial behaviour through modelling.

items.stem: With reference to Cialdini et al. (1987), explain how research has investigated egoistic explanations of prosocial behaviour.
items.answer: Cialdini et al. (1987). Aim: to test whether empathic helping is explained by the desire to relieve one's own sadness. Method: Participants exposed to a person in need were given an opportunity to help; in some conditions they were led to believe that their mood was "fixed" by a drug (so helping could not improve it) or received a mood-lifting reward first. Findings: when participants believed helping could not improve their mood, or their mood had already been lifted, the link between empathy and helping weakened Link: egoistic explanations of prosocial behaviour.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for accurate description of the study (aim, method, findings: when participants believed helping could not improve their mood, or their mood had already been lifted, the link between empathy and helping weakened); up to 2 marks for explicitly linking the findings to egoistic explanations of prosocial behaviour. items.stem: With reference to Latané and Darley (1968), explain how research has investigated pluralistic ignorance in bystanderism.
items.answer: Latané and Darley (1968). Aim: to investigate whether the presence of others affects reporting a possible emergency. Method: Students completed a questionnaire in a room as smoke poured in through a vent; they were alone, with two passive confederates, or in groups of three naive participants. Findings: 75% of participants alone reported the smoke, compared with 10% of those with passive confederates and 38% of naive groups Link: pluralistic ignorance in bystanderism.

items.stem: Describe the study by Batson et al. (1981) and explain what it shows about the empathy-altruism hypothesis.
items.answer: Batson et al. (1981). Aim: to test whether empathic concern produces altruistic helping even when escape is easy. Method: Female students watched "Elaine" (a confederate) apparently receiving electric shocks; empathy was manipulated by similarity information and escape was easy or difficult. Participants were offered the chance to take her place. Findings: high-empathy participants offered to take Elaine's place even when escape was easy, whereas low-empathy participants helped mainly when escape was difficult Link: the empathy-altruism hypothesis.
